cp-cardiac-pathophys: At what point does myocardium become ischemic?
When metabolic demand for oxygen exceeds supply
How can abnormalities of the microcirculation produce cardiac ischemia?
Endothelial cells in small vessels regulate the vasculature abnormally
Which are PROBABLE rather than major risk factors?
Male sex, homocysteine and high sensitivity C reactive protein
What is homocysteine?
An intermediary amino acid formed converting methionine to cysteine
Which lipoprotein carries the highest risk, and why?
Low density lipoprotein, because it is high in cholesterol
What is the molecular defect in familial hypercholesterolemia?
A defective low density lipoprotein receptor on liver cells
What initiates atherosclerotic plaque formation?
Injury to the endothelial cells of the vessel
What is a foam cell?
A lipid-filled macrophage
What is the significance of a large lipid core within a plaque?
Plaques with large lipid cores are fragile and rupture
What follows exposure of subendothelial proteins when a plaque ruptures?
Platelet aggregation and thrombus formation
What makes a plaque more stable over time?
Collagen and fibrin forming a cap
How do the capillaries within the atherosclerotic arterial wall contribute to disruption?
Their thin walls bleed
What is the immediate metabolic consequence of reduced oxygen supply to cardiac cells?
The formation of adenosine triphosphate falls
Why does slowly progressive plaque formation allow the heart to tolerate more narrowing?
Collateral circulation develops over the years the plaque is growing
How are the coronary syndromes classified?
By the severity and onset of cardiac symptoms
What distinguishes angina pectoris from infarction at the cellular level?
The ischemia is intermittent and insufficient to kill cardiac cells
What is the mechanism of stable, typical angina?
Stenotic vessels reduce flow to a critical level
Why is unstable angina included among the acute coronary syndromes?
It may progress to acute ischemia
What do unstable angina and myocardial infarction share?
Pain lasting longer than typical angina
Following complete occlusion, in what order do the cellular changes occur?
Depleted energy, then failed contraction, then necrosis
Where are nearly all myocardial infarcts located, and which artery is most often responsible?
The left ventricular walls, most often the left anterior descending
How does valvular stenosis change the work the heart does?
It imposes extra PRESSURE work
What sequence follows the raised left atrial pressure of mitral stenosis?
Atrial enlargement and hypertrophy
What happens in mitral regurgitation?
Blood flows back from ventricle to atrium during systole
What is mitral valve prolapse?
Ballooning of the valve into the left atrium during systole
What is the most common cause of aortic valve stenosis?
Calcification occurring with aging
What happens in aortic regurgitation?
Blood leaks back into the left ventricle from the aorta during diastole
By what mechanism does rheumatic fever damage the heart?
An immune attack arising from cross-reactivity after streptococcal infection
What is a prerequisite for infective endocarditis?
Invasion of the bloodstream by the organism
Why does subacute infective endocarditis require pre-existing valve pathology?
Its organisms are not virulent enough to attack a healthy endocardium
What characterizes myocarditis pathologically?
Inflammation, leukocyte infiltration and necrosis
What does the Frank-Starling law state?
The more the ventricle fills during diastole
What defines dilated cardiomyopathy?
Cardiac failure with dilation of one or both ventricular chambers
Why is a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy symptomatic?
Ventricular outflow obstruction and impaired diastolic filling
cp-vascular-pathophys: Which four functions does the vascular system serve?
Transport of nutrients, wastes, hormones; homeostasis
What does the pulmonary loop do?
Carries deoxygenated blood from the right heart to the lungs
What characterizes the arteries?
High pressure, strong walls, high flow velocity
What does the intima consist of?
A single layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane
How does capillary diameter compare with a red blood cell?
Equal to or even slightly smaller
What kind of epithelium lines the vessel lumen?
Specialized simple squamous epithelium
Which layer are smooth muscle cells the predominant element of?
The media
What does vascular injury with endothelial dysfunction or loss stimulate?
Smooth muscle recruitment and proliferation into the intima
Which are the four principal mechanisms of vascular disease?
Weakening, narrowing, dilation and rupture
Why do vascular disorders affect specific types of vessel?
Each vessel type is built for its own physiologic needs
Which disease process affects the large elastic arteries?
Aneurysm
What two quantities determine blood pressure?
Vascular resistance and cardiac output
What triggers renin secretion?
A fall in pressure in the afferent arterioles
What proportion of hypertension is idiopathic?
About 90 to 95 percent
By what mechanism does renal artery stenosis raise blood pressure?
Reduced glomerular flow and afferent pressure induce renin secretion
What does arteriosclerosis mean?
Arterial wall thickening with loss of elasticity
What burden does atherosclerosis carry in the Western world?
More morbidity and mortality than any other disorder
What is the structure of an atheroma?
A soft lipid core with a fibrous cap
What is an aneurysm?
Localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel
Where do atherosclerotic aneurysms occur most commonly?
The abdominal aorta and iliacs
What happens to the aortic wall in dissection?
The laminar planes of the media split apart
What characterizes a saccular cerebral aneurysm?
A thin-walled protrusion lacking elastic lamina
What happens to the vessel wall in fibromuscular dysplasia?
Segments are focally thickened by hyperplasia and fibrosis
What is vasculitis, and which vessels does it mostly affect?
Wall inflammation, mostly small vessels
What is Raynaud phenomenon?
An exaggerated vasoconstrictive response
What is an arteriovenous fistula?
A direct connection between an artery and a vein
What proportion of the body's total blood volume do the veins contain?
About 66 percent
What causes varicose veins?
Chronic high intraluminal pressure
Where does deep vein thrombosis rank among cardiovascular causes of death?
Third most common
What are the three components of the Virchow triad?
Wall damage, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability
What is the role of the arterioles?
Control conduits for release of blood to the capillaries
How is the media of an elastic artery such as the aorta arranged?
In lamellar units of elastin and smooth muscle, like tree rings
Why does the capillary bed favor exchange?
Thin walls combined with slow flow
What does a nonthrombogenic endothelial surface achieve?
It keeps blood in a fluid state
cp-immunity: What are the three functions of immunity?
Defense against invaders, surveillance for mutant cells, homeostasis by removing debris
What does immunological memory provide on re-exposure?
A faster, stronger adaptive response to the same antigen
What do B-cell and T-cell receptors recognize?
Particular epitopes on an antigen
What defines passive immunity?
Transfer of preformed antibodies from another source
How long does passive immunity protect?
Immediately, then declines as the transferred antibodies are lost
Which antibody gives natural passive immunity across the placenta?
Maternal IgG
Which antibody in breast milk gives natural passive immunity?
IgA
What is artificial active immunity?
Antigen exposure on purpose: vaccination
What defines innate immunity?
Defenses that act without prior sensitization to a particular antigen
Which white cell is the most numerous first responder?
The neutrophil
Which granulocyte handles allergic reactions and parasites?
The eosinophil
Which blood granulocyte resembles the tissue mast cell?
The basophil
What does a monocyte become in tissue?
A macrophage (a tissue macrophage is a histiocyte)
Where do T cells mature?
In the thymus
How do natural killer cells differ from cytotoxic T cells?
They need no specific antigen to recognize a target
What starts the antigen-dependent phase of B-cell maturation?
Exposure to the antigen
Which cell actually produces antibody?
The plasma cell, transformed from a B cell
Which antibody class rises first in a primary response?
IgM
Which antibody class dominates the secondary response?
IgG
What forms an antibody's antigen-binding site?
The heavy- and light-chain variable regions together
What decides an immunoglobulin's class?
The heavy-chain constant region
Which antibody region carries out effector functions?
The Fc region
Which immunoglobulin is a pentamer when secreted?
IgM
Which immunoglobulin makes up 75 to 80% of serum antibody?
IgG
Which immunoglobulin binds mast cells and basophils?
IgE
What does antibody neutralization do?
Blocks an essential interaction without destroying the particle
What does opsonization do?
Coats the antigen so phagocytes ingest it more easily
Why is group O the universal red-cell donor?
Its red cells carry neither A nor B antigen
Which T cell reads major histocompatibility complex class II?
The CD4 helper T cell
How do cytotoxic T cells kill their targets?
Perforin and granzymes trigger target-cell apoptosis
What do regulatory T cells maintain?
Self-tolerance, by limiting immune activation
What sorts hypersensitivity into types I to IV?
The immune mechanism, not the severity
What mediates type I hypersensitivity?
IgE fixed on mast cells and basophils
What mediates type II hypersensitivity?
IgG or IgM bound to antigens on cells or tissue
What mediates type III hypersensitivity?
Antigen-antibody complexes deposited in tissues or vessels
What mediates type IV hypersensitivity?
Sensitized CD4 or CD8 T cells, over 24 to 72 hours
Where do all complement pathways converge?
On C3 activation
Which complement components form the membrane attack complex?
C5b with C6 to C9
What does X-linked agammaglobulinemia impair?
B-cell maturation, so antibodies are very low
What causes secondary immunodeficiency?
Disease, medications, malignancy or inadequate nutrition
cp-pulmonary-pathophys: What is hypoxia?
Decreased oxygenation of the tissues
What is hypoxemia?
Decreased oxygen in the blood
What PaO2 (arterial oxygen tension) marks acute respiratory failure on room air?
Below 60 mmHg
What PaCO2 (arterial carbon dioxide tension) marks acute respiratory failure?
Above 50 mmHg
What pattern defines hypoxic respiratory failure?
Hypoxemia with normal or low carbon dioxide
What does pulmonary embolism add that causes hypercapnia?
Increased dead space (wasted ventilation)
How do fever and burns push toward hypercapnic failure?
They raise carbon dioxide production
What is the normal mean pulmonary arterial pressure?
About 15 mmHg
How does chronic hypoxic lung disease raise pulmonary resistance?
Hypoxic vasoconstriction of the pulmonary arteries
How does mitral stenosis cause pulmonary hypertension?
It raises left atrial pressure
What defines pulmonary hypertension?
Mean pulmonary arterial pressure at rest above 20 mmHg
Which lung cancer doubles fastest?
Small cell carcinoma, in about 33 days
Which lung cancer is most common?
Adenocarcinoma, 35 to 40% of cases
Why is squamous cell lung cancer found earlier?
It is central, so sputum cytology can show it
What defines obstructive pulmonary disease?
Increased resistance to airflow
What makes asthma different from other obstructive diseases?
Its obstruction is reversible
What mediates the immediate phase of allergic asthma?
IgE on mast cells
Which mast-cell mediators are the slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis?
Leukotrienes
What lab pattern fits non-allergic asthma?
Negative skin tests and normal serum IgE
What lies beneath the basement membrane in asthma?
Collagen deposition
What cough pattern defines chronic bronchitis?
Productive cough over 3 months a year for 2 years
What replaces ciliated epithelium in chronic bronchitis?
Squamous cells
What does the label blue bloater reflect?
Cyanosis and the edema of right-sided heart failure
What is cor pulmonale?
Right ventricular dilation caused by lung disease
What defines emphysema?
Destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis
What does alpha-1 antitrypsin normally do?
Inhibits proteolytic breakdown of alveolar tissue
Why does lost lung tissue narrow airways in emphysema?
Radial traction that holds airways open is lost
Which emphysema type destroys the respiratory bronchioles?
Centriacinar (centrilobular)
What does a low FEV1/FVC ratio identify?
Expiratory airflow limitation
What is the basic lesion of bronchiectasis?
Destroyed bronchial walls that leave the bronchi dilated
What defines restrictive lung disease?
Decreased expansion of the lungs
Which finding confirms a restrictive pattern?
Low total lung capacity
Which alveolar pattern of interstitial lung disease is reversible?
Inflammation, the early pattern
What is the characteristic lesion of sarcoidosis?
Noncaseating epithelioid granulomas
Antibodies to inhaled particles in hypersensitivity pneumonitis cause which hypersensitivity type?
Type III
What is a pneumoconiosis?
Lung disease from inhaled inorganic dust
What starts acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Damage to the alveolar-capillary membrane
Why do alveoli collapse in acute respiratory distress syndrome?
Lack of surfactant
What ruptures in a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
Small subpleural blebs at the apices
Why does tension pneumothorax cut cardiac output?
The shifted mediastinum reduces venous return
What mechanism produces a transudative effusion?
Raised hydrostatic or lowered oncotic pressure
Which LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) ratio marks an exudate?
A pleural to serum ratio above 0.6
What is a chylothorax?
Chyle leaking from the thoracic duct into the pleura
What separates obstructive apnea from central apnea?
Respiratory effort continues while airflow stops
What does gross aspiration deliver to the lungs?
Large numbers of anaerobic bacteria
How do late-onset hospital pneumonias differ?
They are more often multidrug-resistant
